clinician.trajectory_summary: A 31-year-old female presented in November 2020 with a 10-month history of left-sided pulsatile tinnitus that had been previously misdiagnosed as migraine and subjective tinnitus at tertiary hospitals. Physical examination showed that the tinnitus was reduced with internal carotid artery compression but not affected by internal jugular vein compression, and there were no ocular symptoms or abnormalities. Initial three-dimensional time-of-flight (TOF) MR angiography on admission revealed a small hyperintense signal region at the lesser sphenoid wing (SW) and left para-cavernous sinus (para-CS) region with efferent drainage to the superior ophthalmic vein (SOV), inferior ophthalmic vein (IOV), and through meningeal emissary veins to the pterygoid plexus—findings consistent with a dural arteriovenous fistula. The patient declined invasive diagnostics and elected conservative follow-up. At 30 months after symptom onset, the pulsatile tinnitus abruptly ceased without any apparent provocation. A subsequent 3D-TOF MR angiography follow-up examination failed to detect any residual high-intensity signals within the SW region, para-CS, or any of the associated efferent vessels, confirming complete spontaneous closure of the fistula. The tinnitus handicap inventory score decreased from 32 to 0, and the patient reported no ocular symptoms or adverse effects following cessation of the tinnitus.
